title: The one who blinks
hookLine: the gods want Damayanti too, and they make Nala carry their proposal to her
carry: truth alone wins; even gods honor it

cards: Nala is on the road to Damayanti's swayamvara when he meets some travelers who are not travelers at all. They are Indra, Agni, Varuna and Yama, the gods themselves, headed to the same ceremony for the same reason.
They ask Nala for a favor, and he says yes before he knows what it is. Then they tell him. Go to Damayanti, they say, and ask her to choose one of us.
So the man who loves her becomes the messenger for his rivals. And they happen to be gods.

teach.b: Nala has given his word, and he keeps it. By the gods' power he walks unseen past the guards into Damayanti's rooms. I am Nala, he tells her, and I come as a messenger from the gods.

Damayanti doesn't hesitate; she has already given herself to Nala in her heart. Let the gods come to the ceremony, she says, and you come too, and I'll choose you in front of them, so no blame falls on you.
Nala carries her answer back honestly, word for word.
Then the day comes. Damayanti walks into the hall with her garland, and she sees Nala. And next to him, another Nala.
And another. The gods have taken his shape. In her heart she bows to the gods and asks them, by the truth of her vow, to show her who is who.
And they do: no sweat on their skin, eyes that don't blink, garlands still fresh, feet not quite touching the ground. One of them casts a shadow.

teach.h: SHE CHOOSES THE ONE WHO BLINKS.
teach.b: His garland is wilting, there's dust on him, and he blinks. She chooses the one who is only human, and the gods bless the pair with gifts. Now the teaching.

Neither of them wins by a trick. Nala keeps his word against his own heart; Damayanti calls on the truth of her vow, and the gods answer. That's satya, truth, among the highest values in Hindu teaching.
The Mundaka Upanishad says it in three words, satyameva jayate: truth alone wins. India took them as its motto.
For today: when a small lie would make things easier, Hindu teaching says truth has a power even the gods honor.

how: The scene of Damayanti choosing the human Nala among the gods is part of the Nala story in the Vana Parva of the Mahabharata, which a sage tells to Yudhishthira in the forest.

games.q: you're Damayanti. you walk in with your garland and see several Nalas, all the same. what do you do?
o: in your heart, ask the gods by the truth of your vow to show who is who.
leave the hall and refuse to choose.
games.why: she appeals to the gods by the truth of her vow; they show their marks, and she garlands the one who casts a shadow. satya, truth, is a power even the gods honor.

practice: Bring to mind one place where a small untruth has been tempting: an excuse, a stretched story, a 'fine' that isn't. Breathe in and say inwardly, satyam, truth; breathe out and let the easier version go.
If you pray, ask for Nala's courage, to carry a true message even when it costs you; if not, simply rest with the word.

wordCard.voice: Nala. The king who carries his rivals' message honestly, and is found among the gods because he sweats, blinks, and casts a shadow.

orig.note: Sanskrit Nala, the king of the Nishadhas whose story the sage tells in the forest.

carryVoice: Your line: truth alone wins; even gods honor it. Dust, sweat and a blink were how she knew him. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Nalopakhyana: the gods meet Nala; Nala as messenger; Damayanti's answer; the swayamvara and the marks of the gods)
Mundaka Upanishad 3.1.6 (satyameva jayate, 'truth alone wins'), India's national motto; satya as a central Hindu value
